newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Dutch call money eases but deposit rates stay firm.
newsitem.headline: Dutch call money eases but deposit rates stay firm.

text.p: Dutch call money retreated from its recently reached high level on Wednesday afternoon, as banks had sorted out their positions.
Call money was bid between 3.12 and 3.25 percent around 1330 GMT, down from 3.25 to 3.50 on Tuesday.
Dealers said overnight money had edged higher as the strong dollar had stirred up fears of a hike in Germany's repo rate, but they played down the likelihood at of such a move.
"That's just some unnecessary panicking," one dealer said.

He said some summer staffing problems meant many market participants had less experienced staff working with the new money market instruments, adding this might be behind the rates' recent rise as well.

"It just takes the smaller banks some extra time to sort out their positions, so rates are higher than usual in the morning and then ease in the afternoon when the small ones get out of the market and only the big ones remain," he said.
Most deposits were unchanged from Tuesday, with one-month deposits quoted at 3.18/26 percent, six-months at 3.26/34 percent and one-year deposits set at 3.30/34 percent.
German deposits between one month and one year traded slightly higher than on Tuesday.

Indicative prices for Dutch Treasury Certificates (DTCs) remained quite defensive at 3.16 percent for DTCs maturing in August and September. December paper was set at 3.17 percent, and DTCs running until June 1998 at 3.25 percent.
The guilder was virtually unchanged against the mark, trading at 112.56 per 100 marks.
